quote: **Thiamine parenterally, before dextrose** [12]. Replete **magnesium** and potassium.
problem: The page names Wernicke encephalopathy as a can't-miss ("classic triad present in a minority — most cases are missed") and then gives only route and sequence, never distinguishing prophylactic from treatment thiamine dosing. The order a resident actually writes is thiamine 100 mg IV daily; that is a prophylaxis dose and does not treat suspected Wernicke. In a malnourished, delirious DT patient this is the standard route to a permanent Korsakoff amnestic syndrome, and the page cites a review whose whole subject is guideline thiamine dosing [12] while omitting the dose.
replacement: **High-dose parenteral thiamine, before dextrose** — this is a *treatment*, not a prophylaxis, indication: suspected Wernicke encephalopathy is treated with parenteral thiamine on the order of 500 mg IV three times daily for 2–3 days, followed by a reduced parenteral course, per institutional protocol. The reflexive 100 mg IV daily order is a prophylactic dose and does not treat Wernicke [12]. Replete **magnesium** and potassium — magnesium is an obligate cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes, so thiamine will underperform until his magnesium of 1.4 is corrected.
basis: EFNS guideline on diagnosis and management of Wernicke encephalopathy (2010) and BAP / Royal College of Physicians guidance specify high-dose parenteral thiamine (commonly 500 mg IV tds) for suspected or established WE, versus roughly 250 mg daily for prophylaxis in high-risk AUD inpatients. The page's own reference [12] (Pruckner 2019) is a review of exactly this guideline variation. Magnesium as a cofactor for transketolase and other thiamine-dependent enzymes is standard.

quote: > Two opposite toxidromes in one encounter: opioid overdose reversed by naloxone, then precipitated withdrawal - and why buprenorphine has to be started in withdrawal.
problem: Two defects in the card the learner reads before the page. (1) It describes a case that does not exist: there is no opioid overdose and no naloxone anywhere in this stem — the patient presents with vertebral osteomyelitis and a day-1 buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal. (2) "buprenorphine has to be started in withdrawal" states as an absolute rule the exact reflex the page is written to correct: Q1 teaches that COWS-threshold initiation is unreliable in fentanyl-exposed patients, and Q2–Q3 teach that low-dose (Bernese) initiation deliberately avoids any withdrawal window by escalating buprenorphine while the full agonist continues. A resident who takes the overlay as the rule will insist on a withdrawal window in a fentanyl-exposed patient — which is the day-1 error — or will withhold buprenorphine from a patient who cannot tolerate one.
replacement: > One encounter, two failures: a COWS-threshold buprenorphine start precipitated withdrawal in a fentanyl-exposed patient, and the recovery is methadone or low-dose initiation - with acute pain treated alongside the MOUD, never instead of it.
basis: The page's own Q1–Q3 and refs [2,3,5,6,7]. Low-dose/Bernese initiation is defined by continuing the full agonist rather than requiring a withdrawal window; standard-initiation COWS thresholds are explicitly described on this page as less reliable in the fentanyl era.

quote: Teaching takeaway: Two opposite toxidromes in one encounter: opioid overdose reversed by naloxone, then precipitated withdrawal - and why buprenorphine has to be started in withdrawal.
problem: The same string as RV10-F002, rendered a second time as the end-of-case "Teaching takeaway" card: the phantom naloxone-reversed overdose, and the absolute rule that buprenorphine must be started in withdrawal, which contradicts this page's own teaching on low-dose initiation in the fentanyl era. Listed separately because fixing the TL;DR alone leaves the summary card still teaching the error.
replacement: Teaching takeaway: One encounter, two failures: a COWS-threshold buprenorphine start precipitated withdrawal in a fentanyl-exposed patient, and the recovery is methadone or low-dose initiation - with acute pain treated alongside the MOUD, never instead of it.
basis: Same as RV10-F002 — the page's Q1–Q3 and refs [2,3,5,6,7]; and the stem, which contains no overdose and no naloxone.

quote: DSM-5-TR *alcohol withdrawal, with perceptual disturbances*, meeting criteria for a withdrawal delirium
problem: This mislabels delirium tremens, and is self-contradictory within one clause. In DSM-5-TR the "with perceptual disturbances" specifier on alcohol withdrawal applies only when hallucinations with intact reality testing, or illusions, occur *in the absence of a delirium* (ICD-10-CM F10.232). The diagnosis here is alcohol withdrawal delirium, a substance withdrawal delirium (F10.231). On a page that states it assumes DSM-5-TR fluency, this teaches a resident to document and code the lower-acuity alcoholic-hallucinosis picture for a patient in DT, collapsing the hallucinosis-versus-DT distinction that drives level of care and the urgency of the handoff.
replacement: DSM-5-TR **alcohol withdrawal delirium** — a substance withdrawal delirium (ICD-10-CM F10.231), *not* alcohol withdrawal "with perceptual disturbances", a specifier reserved for hallucinations or illusions with intact reality testing occurring in the **absence** of delirium
basis: DSM-5-TR, Alcohol Withdrawal diagnostic criteria and specifier text; DSM-5-TR Substance/Medication-Induced Delirium; ICD-10-CM F10.231 (withdrawal delirium) versus F10.232 (withdrawal with perceptual disturbance).

quote: a real reason to favor a controlled barbiturate load over an open-ended benzodiazepine escalation here [7]
problem: This turns probable cirrhosis into an affirmative argument for phenobarbital, and it contradicts the first half of its own sentence ("prefer lorazepam/oxazepam"). Phenobarbital is substantially hepatically metabolised; its half-life is already roughly 80–120 h and is further prolonged in hepatic impairment; it has no reversal agent; and it is a potent sedative that can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy exactly as benzodiazepines can. Hepatic impairment is a reason for more caution with a barbiturate load, not less. A resident acting on this will load phenobarbital in a cirrhotic patient believing it is the hepatically safer choice, and will have no way to titrate back when the sensorium worsens.
replacement: a real reason to avoid open-ended benzodiazepine escalation — but not, on hepatic grounds, an argument *for* phenobarbital: phenobarbital is partly hepatically metabolised, its already long half-life (~80–120 h) is further prolonged in cirrhosis, there is no reversal agent, and it can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy just as benzodiazepines can. If phenobarbital is used here it is because the withdrawal is benzodiazepine-resistant, and it must be used expecting a longer and less reversible effect than in a patient with normal hepatic function [7]
basis: Phenobarbital pharmacokinetics: elimination half-life ~80–120 h in adults, roughly half cleared by hepatic metabolism (CYP2C9/2C19), prolonged in hepatic impairment. Standard AWS-in-liver-disease teaching (and ref [7], Chand 2022) supports lorazepam/oxazepam for their glucuronidation route and warns about sedative-precipitated HE; it does not establish phenobarbital as HE-sparing. Checking whether ref [7] actually endorses barbiturate loading in alcohol-related liver disease would settle whether the citation is also mis-attached.

quote: Hypercalcemia can itself produce confusion and contributes to nephrogenic DI. Two lithium effects converging.
problem: A corrected calcium of 10.9 mg/dL is mild hypercalcemia, well below the range at which hypercalcemia produces encephalopathy — neuropsychiatric obtundation is generally a feature above roughly 12–13 mg/dL, and frank encephalopathy above ~14. Presenting it as a driver of this delirium, and ranking "Hypercalcemic encephalopathy" third in the summary differential above uremic/metabolic encephalopathy, mis-calibrates the resident twice: it supplies a false alternative explanation for an encephalopathy that is lithium's, and it invites acute treatment of a calcium that needs none. The contribution to nephrogenic DI is fair; the contribution to the encephalopathy is not. The ranked-differential line ("**Hypercalcemic encephalopathy** from lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism — *concurrent contributor*") needs the same correction.
replacement: Hypercalcemia at this level does contribute to the concentrating defect, but a corrected calcium of 10.9 is well below the range (generally >12–13 mg/dL) at which hypercalcemia produces encephalopathy — read it as a marker of the parathyroid effect and a contributor to her polyuria, not as an explanation for her delirium. Two lithium effects converging, only one of which is driving the neurologic picture.
basis: Standard thresholds for symptomatic hypercalcemia: mild (≤12 mg/dL) is usually asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic; neuropsychiatric features and obtundation appear in the moderate-to-severe range (roughly 12–14 mg/dL and above). Endocrine Society hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia guidance and standard internal-medicine teaching on hypercalcemic crisis.

quote: Mortality is roughly **six-fold higher in the four weeks after opioid agonist treatment stops** compared with time in treatment [9].
problem: This is the figure the page instructs the resident to say to the patient "plainly, as information", so its magnitude is load-bearing. My recollection of Santo et al. 2021 (ref [9]) and of the Sordo 2017 meta-analysis is that the excess in the four weeks after OAT cessation is on the order of two- to three-fold relative to time in treatment, not six-fold. The page's own Q6 restates the same reference as all-cause mortality "roughly half" during treatment versus out of it, which sits awkwardly beside a six-fold figure drawn from the same source. If six-fold is an overstatement, the error lands inside a counselling script.
replacement: Mortality is roughly **two- to three-fold higher in the four weeks after opioid agonist treatment stops** compared with time in treatment [9].
basis: Santo T et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2021 (ref [9]) reports pooled all-cause mortality rate ratios during OAT, out of OAT, and in the first four weeks after cessation; Sordo et al., BMJ 2017 reports approximately 32 versus 11 per 1000 person-years for methadone in the four weeks post-cessation versus in treatment. Reading the rate-ratio table in ref [9] for the "four weeks after cessation" stratum would settle this in one step.

quote: telling a patient in precipitated withdrawal that this is "the medicine working" is both inaccurate and, predictably, treatment-ending
problem: The case is built entirely on a precipitated-withdrawal event and never says what to do while one is happening. The management is counterintuitive and residents get it wrong in the same direction the day-1 team did: buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal is generally treated by giving *more* buprenorphine, promptly and in substantially larger increments, to complete the transition to buprenorphine occupancy, alongside aggressive symptomatic treatment — not by stopping the drug. A resident who learns only that the reassurance was wrong will still stop the buprenorphine, which is precisely how this patient lost her MOUD.
replacement: telling a patient in precipitated withdrawal that this is "the medicine working" is both inaccurate and, predictably, treatment-ending — and the team also needs to know what to do instead, because the correct move is counterintuitive: precipitated withdrawal is generally treated by *continuing and rapidly escalating* buprenorphine to carry the patient through to full buprenorphine occupancy, not by stopping it, together with aggressive symptomatic treatment (antiemetic, alpha-2 agonist, non-opioid analgesia) and full-agonist analgesia where pain requires it
basis: Standard addiction-medicine management of buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal — rescue by additional/escalating buprenorphine plus symptomatic adjuncts rather than discontinuation; the page's own refs [1] (Harris 2026 JAMA review) and [2] (Englander 2024 hospital-OUD review) cover this.

quote: Operationally (framed generally, never specifically): collaboratively engage the patient — and, with consent, a trusted other — to **reduce or remove access to lethal means at home** during the high-risk period
problem: The instruction conflates two different things: not teaching suicide *methods* (correct, and the page's scope note is right to exclude that) and not naming the *specific means this patient has access to*, which is what makes lethal-means counselling work. Effective counselling is means-specific and, in the US, largely firearm-specific: ask what is in the home, then negotiate temporary off-site storage with a trusted person, locking devices, and separating ammunition, plus securing medication supply. A resident told to operationalise this "never specifically" will produce a generic "make the home safe" line that neither changes access nor matches the intervention the page has just called the best-supported strategy in the field. For a Resident audience that carries med-legal accountability for this conversation, it is too thin.
replacement: Operationally — general about *methods*, specific about *this patient's means*: ask directly what lethal means are accessible at home, and collaboratively engage the patient and, with consent, a trusted other in removing or securing them during the high-risk period. In the US that means firearms first (temporary off-site storage with a trusted person, locking devices, ammunition stored separately) and then medication supply (quantity dispensed, lock box). Naming the specific means is what makes the counselling effective; naming methods is neither required nor what this is
basis: Counseling on Access to Lethal Means (CALM) training and the VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide both frame lethal-means counselling as means-specific, with firearm storage as the highest-yield step; Fazel & Runeson, NEJM 2020 (the page's ref [9]) for means restriction as the best-supported strategy.

quote: **Add phenobarbital** per institutional protocol, with an explicit preference for a **loading/replacement strategy rather than open-ended stacking**, given the ventilation and aspiration signal in the adjunct literature [3,9,10]. Airway monitoring is mandatory.
problem: The facilitator notes make "early replacement ≠ late stacked" the single distinction residents should leave with, but the page never states the pharmacokinetic fact that makes the distinction real: phenobarbital's half-life is roughly 80–120 hours, so a load supplies its own taper over days and cannot be titrated back once given. Without that, a resident re-doses on benzodiazepine intuitions, does not anticipate cumulative or delayed sedation on day 2–3, and may run a benzodiazepine taper on top of a phenobarbital load — which is the mechanism behind the ventilation and aspiration signal this very sentence cites.
replacement: **Add phenobarbital** per institutional protocol, with an explicit preference for a **loading/replacement strategy rather than open-ended stacking**, given the ventilation and aspiration signal in the adjunct literature [3,9,10]. The pharmacokinetics are why that distinction is real: phenobarbital's half-life is roughly 80–120 hours, so a load provides its own taper over several days, cannot be titrated back once given, and adds to any benzodiazepine still on board — decide the total load up front and stop the parallel benzodiazepine rather than running both. Airway monitoring is mandatory.
basis: Phenobarbital elimination half-life ~80–120 h in adults — the stated rationale for fixed-load, self-tapering phenobarbital protocols in AWS, and the mechanism behind the additive-sedation harms seen when it is layered onto ongoing high-dose benzodiazepines (the page's refs [9] Kessel 2024 and [10] Cheng 2025).

quote: Plan explicitly for **delivery**, when clearance abruptly normalizes and the risk direction reverses toward toxicity; hydration status during labor matters.
problem: The bullet names the physiology and stops before the management, inside a list the page titles "Practical monitoring changes in pregnancy" and inside a question the facilitator notes rank as one of three priorities. What a resident must actually decide is whether to continue, reduce, or withhold lithium around labour; that a level should be checked at delivery and in the early postpartum; and that the dose returns to the pre-pregnancy dose rather than the higher pregnancy dose once GFR falls — the single most common route to postpartum lithium toxicity. Lactation is omitted entirely, and it is the next question this patient will ask; residents commonly believe lithium is an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding, which is not current practice.
replacement: Plan explicitly for **delivery**, when clearance abruptly normalizes and the risk direction reverses toward toxicity. Decide in advance with obstetrics whether to continue lithium with close level monitoring and assured hydration or to reduce/withhold around labour (practice genuinely varies; reducing toward the pre-pregnancy dose in the 24–48 h before a planned delivery is one common approach). Check a level at delivery and in the early postpartum, and return to the **pre-pregnancy** dose rather than the higher pregnancy dose once GFR falls — this is the commonest route to postpartum toxicity. Counsel on transient neonatal effects (hypotonia, poor feeding), and address **breastfeeding** explicitly: lithium is not an absolute contraindication in a healthy term infant, but it requires a shared decision, infant monitoring, and a plan for infant hydration and levels during illness.
basis: Peripartum lithium management as described in perinatal-psychiatry guidance (NICE CG192 antenatal and postnatal mental health; the Bergink/Wesseloo peripartum lithium literature) and the standard postpartum dose-reversion point given the abrupt fall in GFR at delivery; current lactation guidance treats lithium as usable with infant monitoring rather than contraindicated. Whether to hold or continue at labour varies by centre, so the fix is to state the decision and its options, not to prescribe one.
